narration: Next time you watch an American football game, pay attention to the moment after a hard hit. A player gets up slowly. He shakes his head. And on the sideline, the most advanced brain check in the sport begins: a coach holds up some fingers and asks, how do you feel?
visual_subject: Football game action; the moment after a hard hit

narration: That is it. A guess, dressed up as a medical test. Now imagine that guess simply disappeared — replaced by a headset that watches the player's eyes and finds what his mouth will not admit.
visual_subject: Sideline guesswork: bench assessment + injured player attended

narration: Because that headset now exists. It costs less than three hundred and fifty dollars. It works in about two minutes. And it just beat two thousand, two hundred and ninety-four inventions from around the world.
visual_subject: Headset fitted on athlete outdoors (winners film)

narration: One quick warning before we go further: despite the strange name you will hear — Rumble Rims — this is not about wheelchairs. It is a headset. And by the end of this video, you will know how it reads a brain through the eyes, what it honestly cannot do, and why three students from Harvard built it for the price of a games console.
visual_subject: 'Global Medical Winner — Rumble Rims' card + device on table

narration: Start with the size of the problem, because in America it is enormous. Every year, an estimated two to three million sports concussions happen across the country. Not in professional stadiums — mostly not.
visual_subject: Numbers beat: scale of US sports concussions

narration: On school fields. In youth leagues. In Friday night games in small towns. A United States health survey found that about fifteen percent of high school students — roughly two and a half million teenagers — reported at least one sports concussion in a single twelve-month period.
visual_subject: Youth football fields and Friday-night games

narration: Two and a half million young brains, shaken, in one year. And those are only the ones who reported it.
visual_subject: 2.5 million teenagers figure

narration: Here is the part of this story that should worry every parent watching. The worst damage often does not happen at the moment of the hit. It happens in the minutes after, when a concussed player stays on the field.
visual_subject: Player stays in the game after a hit

narration: Co-inventor Cleo Pontone puts a number on it: playing through a concussion for just fifteen more minutes can make the risk of prolonged symptoms rise twelve times. Twelve times. So the most important medical decision in youth sport is not made in a hospital.
visual_subject: Cleo Pontone interview + game action (12x quote overlay)

narration: It is made on a sideline, in seconds, usually by a coach — with no instrument, no measurement, and a player begging to go back in.
visual_subject: Coach making the sideline call, no instruments

narration: So how does the old check actually work? A trainer asks questions. What day is it. Who are we playing. The player rates his own headache, his own dizziness, his own fog.
visual_subject: The old check: trainer asks questions on the bench

narration: Then comes the problem no questionnaire can fix: athletes lie. Not because they are foolish — because they are competitors. Admitting symptoms means leaving the game, so symptoms get hidden, minimised, joked away.
visual_subject: Athlete talking it down on the bench

narration: The entire system rests on the honesty of the one person with the strongest reason to hide the truth. And a player can pass every question while his brain is already in trouble, because a concussion does not always announce itself in words.
visual_subject: The system rests on the player's honesty

narration: There is, however, one signal a player cannot fake: his eyes. After a concussion, the way the eyes follow, fixate and move changes in ways that can be measured — if you have the equipment.
visual_subject: Eyes as the unfakeable signal: saccade dashboard close-ups

narration: Hospitals and specialist clinics do have it. Clinical eye-tracking systems can read those movements with laboratory precision. But they cost around fifty thousand dollars, they live in clinics, and they help nobody standing on a muddy sideline on a Friday night.
visual_subject: Clinic-grade eye tracking on laptops (the $50,000 world)

narration: So for decades, the rule everyone quietly believed was this: real, objective brain data belongs in a hospital, and the sideline gets the guesswork. Three students decided that rule was backwards.
visual_subject: The rule everyone believed

narration: Meet the inventors. Radhika Saran, Cleo Pontone and Sophia DeVito are second-year students in the Master's in Design Engineering programme at Harvard. Not a medical-device corporation. Not a Silicon Valley giant with a research campus.
visual_subject: Meet the inventors: Radhika Saran interview + students with prototype

narration: Three students, still studying, who looked at the gap between a fifty-thousand-dollar clinic machine and a coach holding up his fingers — and asked the obvious question. The eyes carry the signal.
visual_subject: Harvard campus + the three inventors together

narration: Cameras are cheap. Why does the measurement have to live in a hospital? Their answer is the device at the centre of this video, and it carries one of the strangest names in recent invention history: Rumble Rims.
visual_subject: Prototype parts in hand; winner card close-up

narration: Everything about the design starts from where it will be used. Not a laboratory. A sideline — noisy, rushed, emotional, with a game waiting to restart. So the device had to be portable.
visual_subject: Sideline reality: bench, kit bag, device on table

narration: It had to be fast, because no coach can stop a match for a hospital appointment. It had to give a clear signal, because the person holding it is a coach, not a neurologist.
visual_subject: Fitting the headset on the field

narration: And above all, it had to be cheap enough for the places where most concussions actually happen: schools and community teams, not just wealthy professional programmes. Keep that list in mind — portable, fast, clear, cheap — because it explains every engineering choice that follows.
visual_subject: School and community fields

narration: Here is how it works. The moment a player takes a suspicious hit, he comes off and puts on the headset. In front of him, held at arm's length, is a tablet screen showing a target.
visual_subject: Player puts the headset on

narration: His only job is to follow that target with his eyes. Inside the headset, infrared cameras — mounted at the sides — watch his eyes through a set of mirrors angled at forty-five degrees, a special kind of mirror that lets the cameras see the eyes without blocking his view.
visual_subject: DIAGRAM: eyes -> 45-degree mirrors -> IR cameras -> tablet target

narration: Over a test lasting two to three minutes, those cameras measure precisely how his eyes follow the target, how they fix on it, and how they move between points. The injured brain struggles with exactly these movements — and unlike answers to a questionnaire, eye movements cannot be acted.
visual_subject: Eyes follow/fixate/move: dashboard measurement

narration: The raw camera data then becomes something a sideline can actually use. The system turns those eye movements into a clear screening result on a mobile display the coach can read on the spot. There is also a recovery dashboard, so the player's readings can be followed over the days after the injury, not just in the first chaotic minutes.
visual_subject: Coach-facing display and laptop on the field

narration: And the test produces a report that can be shared with a medical professional — so when the athlete does reach a doctor, the doctor is not starting from the player's own description. The chain is simple: eyes, measurement, report.
visual_subject: Report for the medical professional: laptop session

narration: No single link in it asks the injured player whether he feels fine.
visual_subject: The chain: eyes, measurement, report

narration: Now the number this whole story turns on. The clinical eye-tracking systems in hospitals cost around fifty thousand dollars. The current Rumble Rims prototype was built for under three hundred and fifty dollars.
visual_subject: HERO 1: the $50,000 clinic system

narration: Read that again. Under three hundred and fifty — roughly one hundred and forty times cheaper than the clinic machine. That is not a small discount on the same idea. It is the difference between a technology owned by hospitals and a technology that could plausibly sit in a school team's equipment bag.
visual_subject: HERO 2: under $350 — about 140x cheaper

narration: Price is not a detail in this story. Price is the invention. Everything else — the cameras, the mirrors, the software — already existed. Putting it together at this price, for this place, is what nobody had done.
visual_subject: Price is the invention

narration: The rest of the world noticed on the fourth of November, 2026. That night, the James Dyson Award announced its global winners — and Rumble Rims was named the Global Medical Winner. It was chosen personally by Sir James Dyson from two thousand, two hundred and ninety-four entries, from twenty-eight countries — the largest field in the award's history.
visual_subject: 4 Nov 2026: Dyson announces the Global Medical Winner

narration: The prize: thirty thousand pounds. It completed a remarkable run for the three students. Earlier, the same invention had won the United States national round of the award, with a prize of six thousand five hundred dollars, and it had also picked up a Red Dot Design Award in the medical devices and technology category.
visual_subject: The win call: inventors react; both winners at the table

narration: A student prototype, built for under three hundred and fifty dollars, had beaten professional design teams from across the planet.
visual_subject: Winner card close-up

narration: The day after the win, the three inventors were in New York, demonstrating the headset — photographers from international news agencies captured the team showing exactly how a player wears it and follows the target.
visual_subject: Demonstrating the headset (inventors demo the device)

narration: Coverage spread quickly through American and international media. And notice what this win completes. This channel has followed this award all season: first a low-cost dialysis machine from the Philippines, then a sixteen-cent earthquake sensor that won the global sustainability prize.
visual_subject: Media coverage: news studio screens

narration: Rumble Rims is the third piece — the global medical winner. Three continents of problems. Three answers built for a fraction of the expected price.
visual_subject: Third winner in the series

narration: Now the honest part, because this channel always slows down here. Rumble Rims does not diagnose a concussion. It screens for one. That difference matters, and the inventors themselves are clear about it: a screening result is a warning flag, and the decision about whether a player returns to the field stays with a qualified healthcare professional — not with the headset, and not with this video.
visual_subject: HONEST: headset worn — screening, not diagnosis

narration: Second: this is still a prototype. It is not a finished product you can buy today, and it has not yet been through the full validation a medical tool needs.
visual_subject: Still a prototype: device on the lab table

narration: Third: the two-minute headline deserves one honest footnote — the test itself takes two to three minutes, and any report you see promising instant, certain answers from any device like this is going further than the science allows.
visual_subject: The 2-3 minute test on the dashboard

narration: What exists today is a brilliantly priced prototype with a global prize — not a proven medical standard. Both halves of that sentence are true.
visual_subject: A prototype with a global prize — not yet a standard

narration: Hold those limits in mind, and the possibility is still remarkable. If this device survives validation, the first objective brain check in sport stops being a hospital privilege. It becomes something a school nurse can run.
visual_subject: What changes: objective check on the field

narration: Something a small-town coach can afford. The report follows the player to the doctor. The dashboard follows him through recovery, so returning too early becomes harder to hide — including from the player himself.
visual_subject: Report follows the player: laptop + dashboard

narration: And the same logic reaches beyond sport: anywhere eyes can be tested cheaply, a first screening can happen on the spot instead of days later, in a clinic the patient may never reach.
visual_subject: Beyond sport: the eye test anywhere

narration: The guesswork does not vanish. But for the first time, it has competition.
visual_subject: The guesswork has competition

narration: So what happens next is specific, and it is already written into the team's own plan. First, they will build and test a higher-fidelity version of the prototype. Then they will refine the eye-movement test itself, and validate the device properly — with athletes, with coaches, with trainers, and with medical advisers looking over their shoulders.
visual_subject: What's next: prototype work — sketches and boards

narration: School pilots — headsets in real school programmes — are the longer-term ambition. That road decides everything. If the measurements hold up under that scrutiny, the prize money and the headlines will have been the easy part.
visual_subject: School pilots ambition: youth fields

narration: If they do not, this stays a beautiful idea. The validation results are the sequel to watch for.
visual_subject: The sequel to watch: validation results

narration: So we end where we began: on the sideline, in the seconds after the hit. For generations, that moment belonged to a guess — how do you feel, how many fingers. Now a headset built by three Harvard students, for less than three hundred and fifty dollars, can spot a possible concussion in just two minutes — and it has a global prize to prove the world is paying attention.
visual_subject: Callback: the seconds after the hit

narration: If you are new here, subscribe — this channel follows inventions like this every week, with the honest limits included. And tell me in the comments: if this were your child, your teammate, or you — would you trust the headset's warning and sit out the game?
visual_subject: Closing: winner card + athlete wearing the headset

narration: Or not yet? I read every comment.
